sources.title: Jin Au Kong, Electromagnetic Wave Theory, last edition 2008, PIERS free release 2021
sources.locator: Complete 1,032-page PDF retrieved. Read Chapter 3, §3.2.A printed pp. 292–294; §3.2.E pp. 299–300; and §3.3.E pp. 315–322, including the uniaxial constitutive equations, ordinary/extraordinary modes, optic-axis degeneracy, k-surface geometry, and the neighboring examples/results recorded below.

contents.name: §3.2.A, equations (3.2.1)–(3.2.2): anisotropic constitutive tensors and a uniaxial principal-coordinate tensor
contents.support: The source gives the tensor constitutive form and principal-axis coefficients. The local definition states the exact SI model, temporal/spatial phase convention, and Maxwell symbol used by all later deductions.

contents.name: Example 3.2.1, pp. 293–294: gyrotropic plasma tensor in an applied magnetic field
contents.reason: The assigned bulk branch assumes a real symmetric positive permittivity tensor and positive scalar permeability; magneto-optic antisymmetric coefficients are outside this reciprocal lossless model.

contents.name: §3.2.E, equations (3.2.15)–(3.2.26), pp. 299–300: reciprocity identity and transpose conditions
contents.support: The treatment derives the bilinear source identity and explicitly uses transpose symmetry without complex conjugation. The local proof carries the hypotheses into the bounded-domain form.

contents.name: §3.3.E, equations (3.3.54)–(3.3.71), pp. 315–319: ordinary and extraordinary branches and polarization sectors
contents.support: The textbook identifies the two uniaxial sectors. The local theorem computes the complete 3-by-3 symbol determinant and proves both directions and the repeated eigenspaces.

contents.name: Example 3.3.2, p. 317: negative coefficients can reverse energy-flow direction
contents.reason: This batch assumes positive real permittivities and positive permeability and makes no negative-index or energy-flow-direction claim.

contents.name: Example 3.3.3, pp. 319–320: quarter-wave plate phase accumulation and a polaroid attenuation limit
contents.reason: The assigned examples concern bulk polarization and reciprocity, not slab thickness, reflection neglect, finite-layer phase accumulation, or a lossy polaroid limit.

contents.name: §3.3.E k-surface discussion and Figure 3.3.6, pp. 320–321: ordinary sphere and extraordinary ellipsoid
contents.support: The theorem includes a normalized two-dimensional cross-section for one positive-uniaxial ratio; the exact surfaces and their intersection are proved algebraically.

contents.name: Example 3.3.4, p. 322: gradient normal to an ellipse
contents.reason: No gradient, ray-surface normal, or energy-velocity direction is needed for the determinant and polarization claims.

contents.name: Example 3.3.5, p. 322: group velocity is normal to a dispersion surface
contents.reason: The assigned theorem proves dispersion surfaces and polarization only; it asserts no group-velocity, energy-velocity, or propagation-speed result.

contents.name: §3.3.E, equations (3.3.68)–(3.3.71), pp. 317–318: extraordinary D is transverse while E can be nonparallel
contents.support: The source gives the qualitative field geometry; the local example supplies an explicit amplitude, checks the symbol, and computes the nonzero longitudinal component.

sources.title: Weng Cho Chew, Electromagnetic Field Theory, Purdue ECE 604 lecture notes, 2023–2024 revision
sources.locator: Complete 624-page lecture book retrieved. Read §7.1.2 printed pp. 83–84; Chapter 12 introduction p. 145; §12.1–§12.1.1 pp. 146–148; §12.1.2 pp. 148–149; and §12.2 p. 150. The source uses exp(+jωt), while local statements use exp(−iωt).

contents.name: §7.1.2, pp. 83–84: anisotropic local tensor law and the nonparallel directions of D and E
contents.support: This supplies independent anisotropic constitutive context. The local definition fixes the positive real lossless branch and derives its phase convention directly from the macroscopic Maxwell equations.

contents.name: §7.1.2, pp. 83–84: complex permittivity for conductive anisotropic media
contents.support: The source confirms fixed-frequency complex tensor coefficients are used in phasor models; the local definition separately declares transpose symmetry and makes no passivity inference.

contents.name: §7.1.2, p. 84: spatially nonlocal and time-convolution constitutive response
contents.reason: The assigned reciprocity definition is local in space at a fixed frequency; it makes no claim for spatially nonlocal susceptibility kernels.

contents.name: Chapter 12 introduction, p. 145: lossless reciprocal systems are described as often time-reversible
contents.reason: The example makes no time-reversal claim; its conclusion is only that positive absorption is compatible with transpose-symmetric reciprocal coefficients.

contents.name: §12.1–§12.1.1, pp. 146–148: Lorentz reciprocity derivation for linear anisotropic tensor media
contents.support: The source derives the same bilinear boundary identity under symmetric tensors. Its opposite time convention is recorded, and the local proof rederives the identity with exp(−iωt).

contents.name: §12.1.2, pp. 148–149: reaction reciprocity using a far-field radiation limit
contents.reason: The local theorem uses a bounded C1 domain and the divergence theorem, not an infinite-radius radiation limit or a source-reaction pairing.

contents.name: §12.2, p. 150: lossy anisotropic conductive media can satisfy reciprocity when tensors are symmetric
contents.support: This supports the separation of reciprocity from losslessness. The local oscillator example independently proves its positive work rate.

sources.title: Niklas Beisert, Elektrodynamik, ETH Zürich 2024 FS, complete 176-page lecture script
sources.locator: The complete 176-page script was retrieved. Read §12.1, printed pp. 12.1–12.2 (PDF pp. 142–143), equations (12.1)–(12.10), including the material Maxwell equations, isotropic plane-wave convention, scalar frequency-dependent permittivity, and the printed group-velocity claim.

contents.name: §12.1, equations (12.1)–(12.3), p. 142: Maxwell equations in matter and isotropic constitutive coefficients
contents.support: This is an independent Maxwell and phasor-convention treatment. The source's isotropic real coefficients are not generalized as a theorem; the local definition states its tensor data class explicitly.

contents.name: §12.1, equations (12.6)–(12.8), p. 143: isotropic monochromatic waves and averaged field energy
contents.reason: The plane-wave formulas and energy density in this source use an isotropic medium; this batch proves anisotropic mode sheets and makes no energy-density claim.

contents.name: §12.1, equations (12.9)–(12.10), p. 143: causal frequency-dependent scalar permittivity
contents.support: The source supplies scalar dispersive-response context. The local example imports the exact single-oscillator loss formula and derives the period-averaged work sign itself.

contents.name: §12.1, p. 143: printed universal upper bound on group velocity
contents.reason: No group-velocity or front-speed conclusion is in this pair; the printed assertion is not adopted or used.

canonical.name: Fixed-frequency complex reciprocal tensor model needed to match the planned reciprocity hypotheses
canonical.support: This additional A-page definition distinguishes the general complex transpose-symmetric phasor class from the planned lossless plane-symbol branch and is used by the full conditional reciprocity proof.
